speechtext: The hon. member for Yorkton.

Mr. Speaker, this is another of those unfortunate divorce cases in which there is difficulty in coming to a decision as to what should be

done, and where hon. members have difficulty in deciding whether or not justice has been done.
The evidence is contusing, and to my mind it is certainly far from convincing. It is the type of case I think should not come before the House of Commons, and I must protest again, as we have done on so many occasions, against parliament having anything to do with finding, as a point of justice, whether the person in this instance is guilty or otherwise.
Previous experience in cases of this kind has not been of the best, and some of the evidence presented has been seriously questioned. Another point that causes us some qualms about the decision in this case is the fact that some of the investigators are, I understand, those who were found guilty in an Ontario court of committing perjury, but who later won their appeal to an Ontario appeal court on the ground that the court here is not a court of justice. I believe last year the Criminal Code was amended to correct that difficulty. I still do not think this is a court of justice in the true sense of the term, and I must repeat my protest against the sort of thing that is being done in the committee.
I do not claim to have greater wisdom than judges in the courts, but I do claim that members of parliament, including the members of the committee, are not trained to be judges, and I maintain we should not assume the duty of deciding court cases in circumstances such as these. There are grave doubts in the minds of many members of the House of Commons as to the merits of this case. The defendant has had difficulty in presenting her side of the story. But my main reason for objecting at the moment is that if there is not complete proof of the guilt of the defendant, then serious injustice will be done, not the least of which is the injustice to the children involved.
In this instance nothing has been proved completely. The evidence was presented to the divorce committee of the Senate, and that committee made its decision. The bill is now brought to this house for second reading. In view of the lack of conclusive proof to establish guilt, I must protest against the passage of this bill on second reading.
The only redeeming feature in the situation is that I understand, according to information I received within the last 20 minutes, that this case is being presented to our committee on miscellaneous private bills, and that the defendant will be given an opportunity to come before members of the House of Commons who sit on the committee and present her case. We are willing to reserve judgment 50433-405
Private Bills-Divorce
until after that has been done. It is my hope that when she does appear full opportunity will be given her to present her case completely, and perhaps on that evidence we can come to some proper judgment. Until that is done I reserve my right to oppose the bill on second reading.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, July 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Hunter for the second reading of Bill No. 427, for the relief of Joseph Delphis Guillaume Delorme.

Mr. Speaker, I would remind hon. members that this is the same case which came before the House of Commons about a year ago. After I had reviewed briefly some of the evidence that appeared in the Senate committee report, this house decided by a majority vote that the bill should not be read a third time and referred it back to the miscellaneous private bills committee. I would ask hon. members to follow me rather closely in what I am about to say, so they may decide whether in their judgment a home should be broken on the basis of this evidence.
In one paragraph of the petition it is alleged that-
-your petitioner ever since he discovered that the said Antoinette Seguin had committed said adultery has lived separate and apart from her-
Upon being examined the petitioner alleged that some 17 years ago his wife committed adultery. This of course was denied by Mrs. Delorme, but he stuck to his story upon cross-examination. When being cross-examined he was asked these questions and gave the following answers:
Q. Where did you go in the house?-A. I went in the door, went in the room, and saw the two of them together, and I went away crying.
Q. What?-A. I went away crying.
Q. Did you wake them up?-A. No I did not.
And then, apparently, a couple of years after he alleged that he found his wife in a compromising position, which she denied, and he said that he went away crying. He was asked these questions and gave these answers:
Q. You mentioned that you had forgiven her until she took court proceedings?-A. Well, it is not that I really forgive her, but for the sake of the children I kept my mouth shut.
Q. Even though she had committed adultery you were willing to sleep with her?-A. As I say, for the sake of the children I done everything I could_

Q. But when she asked for $20 a week that was enough?-A. That is the arrangement.
So much for the evidence of the petitioner. Now, the following is the evidence of the paid detectives in connection with the case. The first of these is Mr. Bergeron. He appeared and said he was being paid to do a job. These are questions and answers in his evidence. I shall begin with an answer:
A. We proceeded to check the electricity.
Q. You pretended you were going there to check the electricity?-A. Yes, so we checked every room and Mrs. William Delorme was showing us every place in the house.
Bearing in mind that he had sworn that he checked every room in the house, let us see what he said a few minutes later on crossexamination. These are the questions and answers:
Q. How many bedrooms are there in that house? -A. We didn't check all, we checked only one room.
Yet only a few moments before he said he had checked every room. The evidence continued:
Q. How did you know it was that room?-A. Because she told us that she was sleeping down there.
Q. Did you ask her where she slept?-A. Yes.
Q. And she told you where she slept?-A. Yes, she told us . . .
Of course the respondent, Mrs. Delorme, denied that most emphatically, saying it was most absurd to suggest that a complete stranger who came there representing himself as being there on behalf of the electrical company would be shown rooms and told where everybody slept.
Then this man had something to do with the ladder. Hon. members will recall that this is the case where the evidence hinged on certain evidence procured from a ladder. The witness was asked:
Q. How many of you went up that ladder that night?-A. Three.
Q. You each went up separately?-A. No; two together, and myself alone.
The next witness was Jean Leclair, the second paid detective. On page 33 of the evidence he was asked these questions:
Q. The two of you were up?-A. Yes.
Q. And you mentioned that you were up first?- A. Well, it is a way of talking; I would say the first one. We were going up slowly and sometimes I was putting my foot on his and trying to take a grab of a rung and sometimes I would cross Mr. Nadeau's hand.
Q. But you were up first?-A. I wouldn't say that: sometimes he was maybe a few inches higher than me and sometimes maybe I was higher than him.
Q. Are you telling me that you both went up together side by side.-A. Yes, it is a broad ladder.
Q. How wide is the ladder?-A. It is a big ladder. I don't like to say it is a very tall or long ladder but it is a very wide ladder.
Q. How wide?-A. Maybe two feet.

Q. And the two of you were climbing side by side?-A. Oh, yes. We had done that before.
By the Acting Chairman:
Q. I presume, witness, it is a ladder you have for the purpose?-A. Not exactly. We use it a lot many times but it is a handy ladder around. It is a hard ladder. It is a heavy duty ladder.
Q. Is it made of aluminum?-A. No, it is light wood but big wood, and the rungs are strong with some braces under. It is a big ladder and a strong ladder.
The hearing adjourned until 2 p.m.
Then we have the evidence of the chief of the detective service. He was asked about the one detective who went up alone:
Q. You say you came down and that Bergeron went up?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. And that he came down quickly?-A. Yes. Well, he is never a fast man, but he came down faster than he usually comes.
Then the chief of the detective service was asked about the location of the ladder, and hon. members should follow this carefully:
Q. On what side of the building was the window in question that you looked into?-A. On the north side.	I
Then Mademoiselle Dumas, also on the staff of the detective service, was called. She, of course, did not go up the ladder as one might expect, but she saw everything that happened on the ladder. She was in the car. She was asked these questions:
Q. Now, the night that you went on the 21st, where was the car parked?-A. First of all. we were parked on Dube street in front of the restaurant and then we went up and parked up in front of 10053 Dube street.
Q. You are positive you parked in front of that house?-A. Not exactly in front of the house but just a few feet away.
Q. On which side?-A. On the south side.
Q. Well, we have been told by Mr. Nadeau and the others that the bedroom in question is on the north side. What would you say as to that?- A. I don't know where the bedroom would be.
Q. So on what side was the ladder put up?-A. I can't say exactly.
Q. Well, from the position you were in the car on the south side of the house if the ladder had been on the north side could you see it?-A. I don't know.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that evidence from this type of witness certainly should not be accepted in this chamber this year, as it was not accepted last year.
There are a few additional comments I should like to make. I should like to mention that the elder son of the family, who is in the air force, came to Ottawa a year ago in the hope that he might be permitted to give evidence to save his mother's good name. Unfortunately the Senate committee refused to hear him, on the ground that they had heard all the evidence they wanted to reach a decision. Later on, of course, this young chap was heard by the House of Commons miscellaneous private bills committee.

Regardless of how hon. members voted on the particular proposition, I am sure they were agreed that the young chap gave very good evidence. His younger brother has since been married. It is significant that these two boys are so loyal to their mother. As devout Catholics they are upset by the prospect of having to face for the rest of their lifetime the fact of this divorce, in which the mother in their opinion is unfairly branded as guilty of an offence which in my opinion she disproved very effectively. In my opinion the two sons were good witnesses.
There is another factor that the hon. member for Saskatoon brought to our attention a year ago, which I think is worthy of consideration. At page 6483 of Hansard, June 26, 1954, the hon. member for Saskatoon is reported as having said:
There is a member in the house today, and he is sitting in this house now, who found it necessary to resign from this particular committee because his son happened to be the counsel for the petitioner in this case. May I say that the hon. gentleman acted up to his name in being honourable. He came to me and told me the circumstances and explained why he was resigning from the committee and having nothing to do with the case. I expect he explained to other members of the committee also his son's connection with the case. My sympathy goes out to him in the awkward situation in which he was placed. His decision, of course, meant that he took no part in this case and he was a mere spectator. One can readily understand the awkwardness of the situation because in and about that committee he would naturally meet his son and his son's client, and that is not a very nice situation. However, another gentleman was put on in his place and that particular gentleman happened to be one of those recorded as voting for this particular divorce. Incidentally, may I point out that I asked for a recorded vote on that committee and the names of those who voted for and against can easily be found on the records.
I want to endorse what the hon. member for Saskatoon has said. The members were convinced that counsel for the petitioner was a very able young lawyer, but I am sure in the province of Quebec there are a great many lawyers who are interested in taking up these cases. It is unfortunate that the friends of the father of the counsel should be placed in the embarrassing position where they have to vote for or against a case in which one of their colleague's sons is involved.
I want to thank hon. members who, in spite of differences with members of this particular group, have broken party lines to reach fair decisions. A year ago-

I understand the situation is that the floating part of the drydock has now been sold and in fact is in Seattle. The remainder of the drydock is still at Prince Rupert, and what disposition is to be made of it is a matter which I understand is under consideration by the C.N.R.
The minister knows of no plan to establish a new drydock in Prince Rupert?

I understand-and here again it is a matter for the Department of Transport -that some alternative arrangement for the drydocking of ships is under consideration. However, I am sure the Minister of Transport will be able to provide the details.
Just as a matter of interest, how is it that the Department of Public Works is good enough to step in to pay the deficits; at least that is what I understood the minister to say?

That is correct. It is an understanding that goes back for a great many years, whereby this department pays the operating deficit on the drydock. I do not know what was the origin of the arrangement, but it is under the terms of a subsidies act.

Do you pay it
on any other drydock?
Yes, we also pay it on the Saint John drydock in New Brunswick, and the Burrard drydock in North Vancouver.
I do not wish to labour the point, but I confess that it seems an odd arrangement.
It may be that it has come to an end with respect to Prince Rupert.

I was going to ask that; because otherwise it seems that those who should bear the load are not bearing it and, vice versa, that the Department of Public Works is bearing it when it should not be. However, I do not wish to press the point. Did I understand from what the minister said that this arrangement is approaching an end?
I understand that the floating part of the drydock has been sold, so there is no drydock there.
I meant this whole business of the Department of Public Works paying the deficit on the drydock.

No, I do not think that has come to an end. Under the Dry Docks Subsidies Act we are responsible. There is an item in the estimates dealing with drydock subsidies, the Burrard drydock at North Vancouver and the Saint John drydock.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer to the Hillsborough bridge, across the Hillsborough river to Charlottetown. While I intend to address my remarks to the minister and ask some questions, I realize the minister is as well aware of the facts as I am. I shall make my remarks brief, but I feel that for the information of the committee and those who would read Hansard I should place on record the history of this bridge.
The bridge was built under an agreement signed in 1900 between the federal government and the government of Prince Edward Island. The bridge was completed in 1906. In the agreement the dominion government built the bridge and was also responsible for maintenance. Prince Edward Island paid an annual sum to look after interest on construction costs, and for maintenance. This bridge was to carry rail and highway traffic. Incidentally, the steel part of the bridge is just under a half mile in length, but the over-all length including approaches is about one mile.
The construction of the bridge was completed in 1906. The original narrow gauge railway was replaced by a standard gauge in 1930. Because the standard gauge trains and rolling stock were heavier than the old equipment it was considered unwise at that time to haul freight trains across the bridge. I should point out that the line across the bridge was the connecting link in the rail line between Charlottetown and Murray Harbour. It was considered unsafe to run freight trains of the heavier type across the bridge. With this in mind a line just under 20 miles long was built from Mount Stewart, at the head of the river, to Lake Verde on the Charlotte-town-Murray Harbour line. This routed the heavy freight traffic around the head of the river, but passenger trains continued to run across the bridge.
Nothing further was heard about the structure until 1951. At that time the Canadian National Railways applied for permission to withdraw their lines from the bridge. Permission was granted by the board of transport commissioners. At the same time summer service in that area, between Charlottetown and Lake Verde, was discontinued. However, during the late fall, the winter months and the early spring months a passenger service is provided there. The trains come as far as Southport at the southern end of the bridge, and from there the passengers are brought by taxi to the city, a distance of about a mile, over this same bridge.
Supply-Public Works
In April of this year an order in council was tabled in this chamber transferring control of the bridge from the Canadian National Railways to the Department of Transport. Subsequently the Minister of Transport entered into correspondence with the premier of Prince Edward Island suggesting that the province take over the operation of the bridge. The suggestion was that according to legal opinion they had obtained the agreement had expired because of certain reasons, details of which I shall not discuss now because in these remarks I am trying to be brief.
The premier of Prince Edward Island refused to consider this. So far as the people at home are concerned, they felt that the original agreement of 1900 was still in effect. Finally on July 8 this year the bridge was closed by order of the Department of Transport. When hon. members realize that there are more than 3,000 vehicles per day using the bridge they will realize the extent of the dislocation of traffic which ensued. Fortunately the provincial government was able to take action on the same day to reopen the bridge.
This bridge lies on the route of the trans-Canada highway between Charlottetown and Wood Island, the latter of which is the Prince Edward Island terminal of the ferry service connecting our province with Caribou, Nova Scotia.
This means that a new and modern structure to meet trans-Canada standards will have to be built. It is the intention, I think, to build a causeway. Because it is trans-Canada highway the federal government will pay one-half the cost. That is the standard practice on trans-Canada right across the country. But the original agreement gave our province certain special rights. Because of that it was contended by our people at home that we should get special consideration in the continued bridging of this river, whether by bridge or by causeway.
One suggestion was that when the new causeway is completed, if it is built, the railway should put its lines back over it and abandon the 19.9 miles of line which they operate from Mount Stewart to Lake Verde. There are reasons why this would seem practical. Let me take an extreme example. I can say that in order to run freight from Southport on my side of the river to Charlottetown by way of the existing line around the head of the river would mean a distance of some 40 miles. The distance is not exact but it is approximately correct. Across the bridge, of course, it is a little more than one mile.
The minister is acting in a dual capacity here so far as our province is concerned. He

Supply-Public Works
is interested in this problem as the minister of the crown who is charged with the responsibility of administering the trans-Canada highway. He is also the man who speaks for our province at the cabinet level. That is one reason I am raising the question now.
As I said, I know he is aware of the problem because I have discussed it with him a number of times recently. I know he is in very close touch with the premier, because I too have been in very close touch with the premier in the last few days. Both of us have tried to emphasize the gravity of the situation to the minister and the urgent need of getting a decision if one is possible. At his own suggestion the minister said he would discuss this very important problem at a high level conference. I believe he does realize the importance of this matter so far as our province and my constituency are concerned. I am wondering whether the minister has anything he can tell me as to the results of his efforts thus far?

This matter of the Hillsborough bridge has been concerning those of us who have been responsible for the administration of the Trans-Canada Highway Act ever since that statute was put on the books. We have been discussing with the government of Prince Edward Island the route of that highway. This bridge became an essential link in the trans-Canada highway in that it means access to the city of Charlottetown.
Under the agreement any part of the trans-Canada highway becomes eligible for 50 per cent participation by the federal government to the cost of construction. But, as my hon. friend has said, there seemed to be a federal interest here going beyond its interest in the trans-Canada highway, by virtue of the fact that this bridge came into being in the first instance as the result of an agreement signed in 1900 between the then minister of railways and canals and the premier of Prince Edward Island. The bridge is no longer safe for railway traffic, which has been discontinued. But it is worth noting that if there were a suitable causeway, or a replacement for the present bridge, it would also serve the interests of the Canadian National Railways by whatever means they chose to transport passengers and freight.
We have recently had discussions with the Canadian National Railways, the Department of Transport, the premier of Prince Edward Island and our own department, and it was agreed that there is an interest by the federal government over and above the trans-Canada highway interest to the extent of one-third, which leaves two-thirds for the provincial government and the federal government to divide between them under the terms of the Trans-Canada Highway Act. This means in

effect that the federal government is prepared to pay two-thirds of the cost of a replacing causeway or other suitable structure on the understanding that the provincial government will pay the remaining third. I understand from the premier of Prince Edward Island that this arrangement is satisfactory to him and his government.
I thank the minister for that assurance.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words to the minister on this item in reference to dredging. I looked through the estimates and found there was no item covering the subject matter that I want to bring to the minister's attention. If the minister examines his files back over the past few months he will find that different bodies in Cape Breton have petitioned his department to do something about dredging the harbour of the town of Glace Bay. I should like to take a minute to impress upon the minister the need for this particular dredging.
As the minister is well aware, that town has suffered considerably from economic upheaval over the past couple of years, and is badly in need of something that will enable the community to expand existing facilities. While the town of Glace Bay is known as a mining town, I want to impress upon the minister the fact that the harbour of which I am speaking is also a very important fishing centre. The largest sword-fishing industry in Canada is located in that harbour. During the season boats from all over the province of Nova Scotia and from Newfoundland fish out of that harbour. In the six or eight weeks of the fishing season probably 200 boats come in and go out. In addition to that, at that point there are two fairly large fish plants. Markets for the fisheries have picked up considerably, and there could be a great expansion of the fishing industry if the harbour were put in shape to accommodate the craft that could make use of it. Dredging has been a problem for some considerable time, as there were sewer pipes in the harbour at one time. That difficulty was removed some years ago by the removal of those pipes.
When the minister is taking a look at it this time I suggest the work should not be done as it has been done in the past, namely by dredging this year and then waiting for a request for the same operation again next year. In conversation with some people in that town it was brought to my attention

that a couple of miles away one of the large stone collieries have a place where they dump the refuse from the mine. During the season the tides run in the direction of the harbour and all the silt that is dumped over the cliff from that colliery drifts into the harbour. If the minister is going to do something about the dredging of the harbour he should get in touch with the people who are using that spot as a stone dump to try to eliminate the reason for having to dredge that harbour year in and year out.
I do not want to hold up the minister's estimates, but I want to impress upon him that this work has been requested for some time. I do not find anything in the supplementary or main estimates to cover it, but I am sure in the different appropriations in the department there must be some miscellaneous funds that could be used to carry on this dredging operation. There are two fairly large dredges in that area from time to time.
This is not a routine job; this is something that should be done for this community that requires help very badly. As the minister knows, some 800-odd employees were just callously dumped on the streets within recent months and there was quite an upset, and any gesture that could be made by the minister at this time in respect to improving those facilities which in turn would encourage the expansion of small industries located there, such as the fish plants I mentioned and the sword-fishing industry, would be money well spent. Could the minister indicate whether he will be able to undertake this work this year, in view of the fact that there is no item in the estimates?

Mr. Chairman, I am glad to have the views and comments of the hon. member for Cape Breton South on this problem of Glace Bay. We are certainly anxious to do everything that is reasonable, especially in the light of the closure of 1-B colliery. The harbour has been studied, and while doubtless the facilities might be improved they seemed to be adequate for the type of operations being carried on. I hope my hon. friend will be satisfied at this time if I tell him that I shall be glad to consider carefully what he has said and have the whole matter reviewed again.

and I should like to know its cost. I should like to know also the cost of the terminal building, for which there is an item of $261,000. I should like to ask the
minister if he would give the details of item 388 for Toronto harbour repairs and improvements. There is a vote of $721,000 including a revote of $380,000.
The vote for Toronto is $721,000. It is made up as follows: reconstruction of section "R" of the western breakwater, $271,000; dredging three areas between Jarvis and Parliament streets, $450,000.
Is there any prospect of any major extension in connection with wharves there in view of the St. Lawrence seaway going through?

I was in contact with the minister some time ago, and I believe others have been in communication with him, regarding the wharves at Brockville and also concerning certain bridging being done there. Could the minister tell me what the department has in mind at the present time in that regard?

There is nothing in the estimates for Brockville, Mr. Chairman. As my

hon. friend says, the harbour at Brockville has been under study at his request and that of other gentlemen whom he knows well, but we have not reached the stage where anything can be put in the estimates.

Mr. Chairman, before we leave that item with regard to Toronto, am I right in assuming that the policy with regard to the use and development of the Toronto harbour is purely in the hands of the Toronto harbour commissioners under that act?
They have their own statute and act under it; that is correct.

So that any planning in
regard to the expansion of the harbour to take care of any further expected increase in activity because of the St. Lawrence seaway would be purely in the hands of the Toronto harbour commissioners? Do we act on their recommendations or requests in so far as money to develop the harbour is concerned?

Yes; it has been somewhat of a joint approach. There is a Toronto harbour commission, which is composed of citizens in various walks of life, some of whom are appointed by the federal government. The policy to date has been that the commission has requested from time to time that the federal government build certain structures there, and they have been built where they have been considered justifiable, by the Department of Public Works. In most, if not all, instances the commission has taken the initiative.

If I could just leave this thought before we leave that subject, Mr. Chairman:	The Toronto harbour commissioners have sold control of the harbour within what might be called the old city. We now have a metropolitan Toronto executive group covering some 16 to 20 miles of shore line altogether. It might be a good idea to consider expansion of the Toronto harbour commissioners to a metropolitan harbour commission that could assess the problems of the whole greater Toronto area to the best advantage. Perhaps it would be worth while for the minister to bear that in mind in regard to future negotiations or policy.
Yes.

I am not sure whether the minister answered a question I asked on the first item, as to whether any new installation was planned in the lake Ontario region in respect of operating the St. Lawrence deep waterway. I had in mind not only the Toronto area but the mouth of the Niagara

river, where there are the ports of Port Weller and Port Dalhousie. There are no facilities in the Niagara river itself, although it is navigable. Having in mind the prospective industrial development of that area, has the department considered the need for further harbour installations in that section and, if so, what are they?

This seaway development has precipitated a great many requests from virtually every port along the great lakes to have an investigation carried out to determine what must be undertaken to accommodate deep sea shipping. It will take some time for this whole matter to crystallize to determine which ports will become key ports in the operation. That field of activity falls more appropriately under the Department of Transport, because it does relate to shipping.
As I have said before today, the role of this department is largely that of a service department to build structures and works that are requested by some other department of government or are brought to our attention through other channels. The responsibility for trying to assess the relative value of ports and decide which should become important and key ports in the economic role of this country is a function that is beyond the scope of the Department of Public Works as such.

As I read the estimates there is no extraordinary expenditure planned for this year along the line which I have indicated as a possibility. The estimates appear to be fairly consistent with prior years, with no extraordinary expenditures for the kind of ocean shipping which might develop.	[DOT]
The estimate of $721,000 is just for improvements to the harbour inside the perimeter of Toronto bay, as far as the harbour board commissioners are concerned at the present time?
Yes, that is correct.

Mr. Chairman, I spoke to the minister regarding the wharf at Ma-Me-O beach, and the minister promised to look into the matter for me. Could he make a statement on that at the present time?

I have some information on Ma-Me-O beach. What my hon. friend has in mind is the fact that this wharf which was recently built consists of a rubble mound approach and a pile bent headblock. The rubble mound approach deteriorated in some parts during the winter, but the headblock stood firm and is in good condition.
Supply-Public Works
The history of this old wharf is that it was built about 1936, I believe. It was later abandoned, and over the years it decayed to the point where most of it was under water. Last year the department decided to rebuild it. Some settlement was expected and some settlement did take place, because there was at least one unusually severe storm. The damage was not considered to be heavy, and we intend to put the wharf back into good shape.

I am very glad to hear that, because it did not take a big storm to wash it out. As a matter of fact I was looking at it a week ago today. I would say that a length of about 100 feet of the wharf is completely under water. The surface of the ramp is unusable as it is. It will require a complete new top. Also the day I was there I was informed that the ice in the lake this year fortunately went out as the result of an offshore breeze in that area at approximately 12 o'clock noon, and that by 4 o'clock at least 15 feet of it had already been washed away as the result of a small wind. The waves could not have been very high because the ice was still in the lake. I hope the minister, in rebuilding this work-because I think the approach to the pierhead is going to have to be almost completely rebuilt- takes good care to get fairly large-size gravel.
I point out to the minister that immediately after the construction of the causeway, or whatever it might be called, was started last winter, one of the residents of the town came to my home in Wetaskiwin and reported that he thought the gravel that was going in there consisted of from about 50 per cent to 75 per cent clay and sand. I therefore went out that afternoon and took a look at it. I immediately went to Edmonton and reported to the local engineer that in my opinion the dirt content was such that it could not possibly stand up under any waves. I was informed that they had their inspector there inspecting every load of gravel that went into it, and that as far as he was concerned the materials were perfectly all right.
Since then, or at least during the day I was out there a week ago, I was told that the gravel pit from which the gravel was taken had been abandoned a good many years ago by the provincial government because of the extremely high clay and sand content, and because the gravel there was so small that they considered it not fit to use in construction.
I would therefore ask the minister that when they are reconstructing the work they be careful of the materials that go into it, because we should like to see it last the

Supply-Public Works
summer. However, I am still of the opinion that if we get a good break-up in the spring, with a northwest wind, in another year we shall probably have to rebuild the pierhead. Maybe the gravel will stand up until that time. So when they are rebuilding I would ask the minister if he would consider putting in some sort of sloping sides on that pierhead so as to allow the ice to ride over rather than get under the pierhead and push it up on to the shore.
I should like to ask the minister if he would care to comment on the request I made on behalf of the people of Wabamun last night with regard to the replacement of the wharf that had been burned.

From the hon. member's remarks last night I understood that he was referring to a wharf built by the Department of Public Works which was burned and never replaced. I can find no record that the Department of Public Works ever had a wharf at Wabamun lake, Alberta. We have no plans now to build one.
It is very much in evidence. It is just a matter of making a visit there and you will find that is quite so.
Are you sure we own it?
I have been told that. I have no authority for it.
Our records do not show that we own the wharf there.

My information may be wrong, but I have been told by fairly responsible people living in that town that you built it or that your department built it and that your engineer promised to replace it just prior to the 1953 election. I do not know whether or not that has any significance. But on behalf of those good people I want to say-
Have you any evidence to that effect?
I have only their say-so.
Oh, oh.
Of course there is evidence of other things in that part of the country that perhaps could substantiate a person thinking along that line, but the important thing is this-

speechtext: I should like to ask the hon. member if he can name one person who told him that.
I can give the name of Mrs. D. V. Thomson.

Oh, oh.
(Mr. Thomas.]
You know Mrs. Thomson as well as I do. I can give you the name of Mr. Hancock. I think he is the secretary of the chamber of commerce there. I have a letter in my files that I could show you.
Bring it down.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: I should like to know if those people whom you have just named said the public works engineer said he would rebuild it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: I should like to know if those people said the public works engineer promised to rebuild it.

I have a letter from this Mrs. Thomson, who was secretary of the community club; I think that is what they call it. I received that letter a year ago. This year I received one from Mr. Hancock, one of the officials of the chamber of commerce, giving me the same story. I had the same story from two sources. I am only giving it to you for what it is worth. I cannot substantiate it.
What did they say?
They are not worth the paper they are written on.
Mrs. Thomson told me personally and again by letter that the engineer had come out there-prior to my election, of course-and said-
Were you there?
That is not very smart. You mind your own affairs. She told me they had been there. I am only giving this for what it is worth.
She told you they had been there?
She told me the engineer had been there inspecting the wharf after it had been burned, and promised that it would be rebuilt.
I think you had better document your stories a little bit better than that.
This year I received a letter requesting that I press for it again on behalf of the chamber of commerce, and telling me in substance the same story.
But you have nothing from the Department of Public Works telling you that?

No. I tried to get that matter out into the open last year but you turned it down, I think rather rashly, because you did

not take time to get the whole story. I do not want to quarrel with you or with anybody else, but I think if that is the case-and I do not see why these good people would tell me that if it did not have some element of truth in it-something should be done. All I should like to do is ask you to consider the matter on its merits. I should be glad to discuss it with you at any time in order to see if we cannot find out some of the pertinent facts that would satisfy you. Then I would expect to get some assurance that you would do the right thing about it.
I do not know what more I can do. It is a request that has been passed on to me. I am presenting it at its face value. All I should like you to do is to be fair enough to me and to the people of that community to recognize the facts pertaining to it. Then I am satisfied that you will do the right thing about it. The minister said he had no knowledge of the project as being within his department. When the whole thing is revealed perhaps it will not come within his department, but that is not the issue. The issue is whether or not anyone can jump up here, especially a minister of the crown, and demand who said this anl who said that and who wrote this and who wrote that. Let him ask me that and I will tell him where to go. Even if I am a preacher I will tell him where to go. Furthermore, if he does not watch himself we will put him there. We are not going to take anything in this house from any two-bit politician.

Item agreed to.

391. British Columbia and Yukon, $4,419,000.

Supply-Public Works The other item has to do with the dredging of the first narrows of Vancouver harbour. I understand a committee has been established to look into the further development of the harbour that will be necessary to allow deeper draft ships to use it. I have here an extract from a statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on February 25, 1953, having to do with the establishment of a committee to study conditions at the first narrows bridge in order to determine the effect that widening of the channel would have on currents within the harbour. In April, 1953, the name of the committee was changed and it is now called the associate committee on navigational facilities on the west coast. One of the votes under item 391 refers to the Qualicum beach, French creek, improvements, stating that the amount to complete is $31,500, of which $8,000 is a revote. Has the minister any particulars to show what will be the depth at low water in the entrance channel to the boat basin when the project contemplated is completed? He will recall that this item has continued for the last two or three years. Last year I pointed out to him the necessity for a further deepening of the channel before the project reaches completion. Inasmuch as this item indicates that the sum required is to complete the work, I should like to have a picture of what the finished entrance channel will be like.
I have not those details with me. However, there again I will be glad to get the information and see that the hon. member is given it.

I would be pleased to have that information, because it is the deciding factor in the over-all usefulness of the harbour. Inasmuch as this amount is for the completion of the work I would like to have some assurance that that has been looked after.
I shall be glad to see that the hon. member gets it.

Item agreed to.
393. To provide for remedial works where damages are caused by, or endanger, navigation or federal government structures and to complete protection works already under way, $700,000.

Mr. Chairman, rivers have been considered boons to any area through which they flow, and certainly the Fraser river of British Columbia is no exception to that rule. However, after admitting that fact we also realize that rivers can cause a great deal of difficulty and many problems as well. In my riding of Fraser Valley there are a number of sections in which the Fraser river is causing considerable difficulty. I believe this is the item under which I should bring the facts to the attention of the minister and ask that further consideration be given to these problems.
A number of times in the past I have called attention to the situation existing in these various areas; and although some work has been done, these problems are of a continuing nature. At the present time, as in the past, we still stand in need of assistance in order to cope with the problem and try to effect some satisfactory solution.
There are three main areas where the problem exists, and I wish to mention them briefly and to refer to communications I have had in connection therewith. The first of

these is at Hope, British Columbia. Some time ago the matter was brought to my attention by some of the old-time residents of the area, who sent telegrams saying their property was in danger. The water had been cutting away at the bank until that property was in danger of being swept away.
From that time we have had communications with the department and have also made personal representations, but up to the present time we have not been able to convince the minister and his officials that this is a responsibility the federal government should assume. I have here a letter from the department dated July 5, after I had brought the matter to its attention. It bears the signature of the deputy minister and says in part as follows:
On the 28th of June the district engineer at New Westminster, B.C., submitted his report covering the bank erosion problem at Hope.
From the lengthy report it seems clear to me that the cause of erosion is a natural action of the river. It may be aggravated, however, by the passage of tug boats close to shore (20 to 25 feet) causing a heavy wash. Another contributing factor is that some of the high bank upstream was bulldozed down to provide a logging truck road at low water level last winter. This latter action, however, while it has speeded up the erosion in the immediate vicinity, is not the cause and would have been done naturally in about one year.
The final paragraph of the letter is as follows:
As there have been no departmental works, either construction or dredging, in the vicinity, which could in any way be said to have been a contributing factor and as the department has no interest in this land, I regret that it cannot assume any responsibility for any protection works.
Following further representations I received another letter from the minister. This letter is dated January 31, 1955, and states in part:
A careful reconsideration has been given to the matter since the deputy minister of the department wrote to you last July 5th, and regret to say that the Department of Public Works cannot accept responsibility for the matter of erosion at this particular point.
As you know, the cause of erosion is the natural action of the river. A contributing factor is that some of the high bank upstream was bulldozed down to provide a logging truck road at low water level last winter. As I see it, erosion at this point is essentially a question of protecting, from the natural forces of the river, river bank property over which the Department of Public Works has no jurisdiction.
And he states in closing:
I am sorry that I cannot give you a more helpful reply in this matter.
I certainly share the minister's sorrow over that fact. Then on March 4 I had a letter from the local member of the legislative assembly, Mr. I. F. Corbett. This letter, dated March 4, 1955, states in one paragraph:
I would also like to state that the minister's reference to the road as a contributing factor to
Supply-Public Works
river erosion is, to me, to say the least, foolishness. Just below where this road has been cut down, the village of Hope, for the past few years, has been building or strengthening the river bank with large stumps and boulders that have been taken from various portions of the streets. The majority of the complaints of the river cutting away the people's property come from below this point from 200 yards to half a mile.
Then finally his very conclusive letter from the minister under date of March 16:
I wish to acknowledge receipt of your letter of March 9, 1955, concerning river bank erosion at Hope, B.C.
This matter has been carefully looked into by this department, and the conclusion is still the same as stated in my letter of January 31, 1955. 1 pointed out that this erosion was mainly due to natural causes and was, therefore, not the responsibility of this department.
I regret that we cannot assist you in solving this problem.
This letter is signed "Robert H. Winters".
I should like to call attention to this fact once again, that no matter what the engineers may say about the situation there, the navigation does have a very definite effect on this situation. The residents who have been living there for years, right at the river bank, have watched the problem develop and have seen it become aggravated, and they are confident that navigation does have a very definite effect upon the erosion problem existing in that area. I would request the minister to make some further attempt to look over the situation, because I feel that as it is a navigable river up to and beyond that point, the federal government certainly does have a responsibility.
One of the areas where this hungry Fraser river has been taking a terrific toll of valuable farming land is right around the town of Agassiz. This is the area in which the Department of Public Works has seen fit to give considerable assistance, and I want to express again, as I have on other occasions, the appreciation of the reeve and the residents of the area as well as myself of the assistance the department is giving in this particular section. I trust that a certain sum has been set aside to assist further in this work. I hope the minister will make reference to it and let us know how much has been allocated for that purpose.
This situation has caused so much difficulty and has cost the municipality such substantial funds that it has about reached a point where it cannot do very much more. It has gotten beyond the capacity of the municipality to solve the problem. They are doing their best; they are putting in as much as they possibly can in order to conserve their property and their area. I suggest that perhaps special consideration could be given. I would like to see the dominion government accept an even greater share of responsibility in

Supply-Public Works
effecting a permanent solution by at least taking care of the whole area so the municipality would have to look after only the maintenance work in the future. I make that suggestion this evening.
The other area where the same problem obtains is at Albion. Again I have had considerable correspondence with the department in connection with this particular area, but so far I have not received any favourable consideration. The attitude taken is that it is just natural causes, natural erosion and is not caused by navigation. I would remind the minister that even although the reports may have been to the contrary, navigation does have a very definite effect upon the problem in the vicinity of Albion, British Columbia.
As I have intimated, there has been no response to our appeal so far. I believe some new proposals will be advanced in the near future; some new requests will be made, and I certainly hope that if the minister and his officials take another look at the problem they will be able to accede to the requests and the proposals that are made to assist in this particular section.
I know this is becoming almost a yearly plea; I suppose it is more than a yearly plea, but we are definitely concerned. The people are suffering great losses, as I have said, of their valuable farm lands in this section. The area between the river and the mountains is so small that they cannot afford to lose very much more. Therefore I would ask the minister and his officials to look the whole situation over again and assist in every way possible in the solution of this major problem.

The minister should make some comment on these questions that have been raised by the hon. member for Fraser Valley. This is a very serious situation in the province of British Columbia. I happen to know from my own personal knowledge that what he has said about the situation at Agassiz is only too true. The municipality of Kent- that is the name of the municipality-is under a tremendous burden in trying to keep up the dikes and preventing the river from eating away farm land there. Can the minister not tell the committee what the government has in mind with regard to works on this part of the Fraser river? I hope he can give the hon. member for Fraser Valley some assurance of favourable consideration to the suggestions that have been made this evening.

I am sure the hon. member has concluded from the long list of correspondence just read by the hon. member for Fraser Valley on this matter that it has already received very exhaustive consideration. The extent of the federal government's

ability to participate is delineated by the wording of the vote. These projects do not fall within the scope of federal jurisdiction. We did participate at Agassiz last year to the extent of some $7,000 on a three-way program with the provincial government and the municipalities in respect of the diking to which my hon. friend has referred.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley said, despite the fact that the engineers do not think the erosion is caused by navigation, he and some of his friends do think so. Well, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra knows the position I must take. We have competent engineers. I think hon. members know that in these instances, if there is any opportunity for the federal government to participate on the ground that the erosion is attributable to navigation, or if it endangers navigation, or if it is caused by any federal structure, then we do come in and participate. In this instance there has been no engineering evidence whatever that the erosion is not due entirely to natural causes.

Does that mean the government is not going to make any contribution toward the work at Agassiz during the present fiscal year? I point out that ships are plying there. For example, there is the ferry running across the Fraser river at Agassiz. The hon. member is quite reasonable in making the suggestion in his statement that navigation has something to do with the washing away of the bank.

We have not been able to find that. In the instance in which we did participate the request came to us through the municipality and the provincial government. To the best of my knowledge we have not had a request for continued participation there and, again to the best of my knowledge, the interests of navigation are not involved.
Would the government not be willing to help during the present fiscal year?

We have no plans to help. There has been no request from the provincial government and the municipality to participate on the same basis, and there are no grounds for the federal government undertaking the work by itself.

Possibly the minister misunderstood, because in one of the letters I read-the letters have been sent to the debates office-there was an admission that navigation did have something to do with it. It seems to me I read that letter, but it was not the only cause.
I believe the hon. member read that letter in connection with his request that something be done at Hope.

That is true, the one at Hope. I thought the minister was speaking of the over-all plea I made when he said his engineers were of the opinion that navigation did not have anything to do with it. Certainly the letter did say that navigation had something to do with it, but it was not the only cause. It did aggravate the situation, and that is why I very definitely think the federal government has a responsibility in this field. Because of the fact that it is navigable water and the boats ply up and down, they aggravate the problem in regard to Agassiz. Perhaps I take too much for granted, but I understood something was included in this vote this year for the Agassiz area. Certainly if there is not the people will be very disappointed, and the request will be made again in the future.

The remarks I wish to make might have been more appropriate on item 389, but I think they will fit in under this item. There was a previous vote for a dock at lie a la Crosse, Saskatchewan. The present structure is in such condition that it cannot be used. In fact you could drive a team through some of the holes. I wonder what happened to the previous vote, and whether it is intended to proceed with this dock?
That item was passed some time ago and I have not the records here. I shall look up the information and give it to my hon. friend.
Item agreed to.

Trans-Canada highway division-
399. Administration, operation and maintenance. $523,395.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say a few words on the trans-Canada highway because it is of great concern to my constituents and to a large number of organizations in the area. The route chosen through the Columbia river basin, which historically

Supply-Public Works
is the Kootenay country, will be oi great importance to the development of the district and to Canada generally.
I might explain to hon. members who are not fully acquainted with the possibilities of the district that the Kootenay country in my opinion is the Koh-i-noor diamond in Canada's casket of natural resources jewels. I do not think anyone can question that. It is a country which is known for its breathtaking scenery and the prospects for revenue from its profit-making resources.
I mention these things briefly because this is not a party question. The question is too big and of too great concern to the people I represent and the people in the surrounding riding for it to be treated in any partisan manner. It has not been treated in that manner in my constituency. I can say that what I intend to say here this evening has the support of a large number of people of all parties in my constituency.
The decision as to the choice of route must be based on a knowledge of the country, on facts, on economics and on common sense. We are very fortunate in this instance in having ample time to make certain that we do choose the correct route through the Columbia river basin in Canada. There have been three major routes under discussion. The first is the Big Bend route, which was constructed largely by the old department of the interior of the federal government and which has been in operation for quite a number of years. The distance on this route from Revelstoke to Mount Eisenhower is about 270 miles. I understand that the provincial government is doing some paving this summer on the western end of this section of the highway.
There is need for this highway for the building of the Mica creek dam; the highway will be needed for the servicing of that dam. I understand from conversations with Americans who were connected with the building of the Grand Coulee dam that a good highway will be needed to carry the enormous tourist traffic which will naturally be visiting such a great structure. I understand that this would be something in the nature of Boulder dam in the United States. We have that route to go on with. It is possible that the provincial government will pave this portion of the road if the Mica creek dam is built. This road will be required even after the dam is built.
Another alternative route is the Rogers pass route, which was the route followed by the C.P.R. The distance from Eisenhower to Revelstoke over this route is 163 miles, as it is somewhat shorter. I should like to direct the attention of the minister to a
[Mr. Herridge.J	I
recommendation which has been made by a civil engineer in my constituency, who at great personal sacrifice of time and some money explored all these possible routes in the interior of British Columbia. I refer to Mr. Affleck of Nelson, who is known all through the southern part of British Columbia. He and two or three other people have spent a great deal of time in exploring these routes.
Only recently in an effort to obtain a firsthand and independent viewpoint on Rogers pass as a route for the trans-Canada highway across the Columbia river basin in British Columbia three members of the interested boards of trade, Hal Bavin of Windermere, Boyd C. Affleck of Nelson and Alex. Jacobs of Kaslo, hiked over the old abandoned roadbed of the Canadian Pacific Railway at Rogers pass. They made a reconnaissance over this route, and Mr. Affleck has drafted his report. I am very pleased to give the minister's department a copy of it. It will be interesting for them, because he is an old-time location engineer. In this report he deals with the difficulties of the route, heavy snowfalls and things of that kind. I am not going into the question of its advantages. That must be determined by final surveys.
As a result of Mr. Affleck's reconnaissance over the Jumbo pass route, a reconnaissance party was established a few years ago, and he and a number of others travelled over the route. The Jumbo pass route, from Mount Eisenhower Junction to Revelstoke, is about 234 miles. It will go from Mount Eisenhower, to Invermere, over the Jumbo pass to the Duncan river to Howser, along Trout lake, then along Arrow lake to Arrowhead and then to Revelstoke. A great deal of enthusiasm has been developed in support of that route. A very good report has been made on it by Mr. Affleck.
In addition to that, last year the provincial government made another reconnaissance survey over the whole route. I understand the route was found quite practicable and has possibilities, but at this time the provincial government is not concerned with recommending it without further survey and investigation. We had those three routes in mind; what the people in British Columbia call the Big Bend route, the Rogers pass route and the Jumbo pass route.
The people in my constituency are particularly interested in the possibilities of the Jumbo pass route. As I said before, this is not a party question. It is a very important question with respect to the development of the Columbia river basin. For the first time in a development of this type, we have time

on our side. We have time to make certain that the final route chosen is the best possible route through the area. Therefore I suggest, Mr. Chairman-and I am being as brief as possible-that there should be a very thorough investigation and survey of all three of these routes as the result of co-operation between the federal and provincial governments.
Generally speaking, according to the terms of the Trans-Canada Highway Act I know the choice of the route is left to the provincial government. But this is a very big question in the interior of British Columbia, and I think the decision in this important matter should be the result of conferences among the federal government, the provincial governments of Alberta and British Columbia and the dominion parks board, and possibly the result of conversations with the Canadian section of the international joint commission. My idea is to have all interested parties cooperate so that when these surveys are completed-and I think a thorough investigation is very necessary of the possibilities of all three routes-the final route will be the best possible one as a result of that coordination of information and possibilities and so on.
That is all that I am going to say in that connection, because I do not want to detain the house any longer; but it is a matter of great importance to my constituency and to all those persons living in the Columbia river basin in Canada. I hope it is approached in a purely non-partisan spirit and that the final result of the co-operation of all parties concerned will be beneficial.

After the hon. member for Vancouver East had spoken last evening in favour of the idea of a system of trans-Canada highways, I said I supported his view in that respect and that 1 would say something more concerning this important matter when the appropriate item came up for consideration by the committee. The appropriate item is here.
I do not desire to say too much or too little about the trans-Canada highway in the western part of Canada. I hope members of the committee will be able to get clearly in their minds a picture of the vastness of western Canada, so they will realize that from, say, Lethbridge in southern Alberta to Edmonton in central Alberta there is a stretch of close to 400 miles, and about midway between those two cities comes the city of Calgary.
It happens that Providence has blessed each of these cities with a pass to the west through the Rocky mountains to the Pacific coast. Just west of Edmonton is the Yellow-head pass, west of Calgary is Kicking Horse
Supply-Public Works
pass, and west of Lethbridge is Crowsnest pass. Each of these passes is apparently designed by Providence to be the location of a road from all of Canada out to the Pacific coast. Each of them has been proposed as the means whereby a trans-Canada highway should go through. The one going through Yellowhead pass has been called the Evergreen highway or the Yellowhead pass highway. The one going through Calgary has been referred to as the Big Bend highway or the Kicking Horse pass highway. The one going through the Crowsnest pass we have been calling the southernmost route or the Crowsnest pass route highway.
In 1947 when we began discussing this matter in this house, with the deep interest of the present Minister of Defence Production, we went into the whole matter with great care. I know he took a deep interest in the problem and still does, and that the minister himself has a deep interest. It is well to remember, I believe, that the welfare of Canada depends upon the maximum development of industry and trade in those two great provinces in the west. In order to have that maximum development of trade between those two provinces, we need all three of those highways. It was thought we should choose one of them to be the particular trans-Canada highway. On the occasion when we were discussing the question in 1947 I held that the southernmost road was the most logical route for the trans-Canada highway. I am still convinced that that is correct.
There are several reasons for that. In the first place it is by far the most direct route from Winnipeg to Vancouver. In the second place it is right along the southern border of Canada. Just as soon as tourists came across the border they would come into contact with this splendid highway and go east or west and, because they would have found a very good highway in Canada where they did not expect to find one, they would therefore be greatly encouraged to travel far and wide into the depths of Canada.
I think this is a very important matter. From the standpoint of trade the area of Alberta and Saskatchewan which would be connected with a corresponding fine area in British Columbia is susceptible of tremendous development. We have for instance great irrigation projects in southern Alberta, with their vast possibilities. Then we have all the fruit growing and lumbering industries and various other industries in British Columbia. I wish to refer to these only briefly, but with sufficient detail to help the committee realize that there is something really big involved here. I could mention other aspects of this matter of the Crowsnest route.
6430	HOUSE OF
Supply-Public Works Last night the minister made a statement which I think did him credit. It was exactly what you would expect the minister to say. May I say that I have the highest esteem for the minister. I do not see how they could find a better man for the job. He said, as recorded on page 6354 of Hansard:
Our first aim and object must be to complete the trans-Canada highway.
That is correct. I agree completely. Now, how to get the trans-Canada highway or, at least, a trans-Canada highway as soon as possible is the first great problem. That would be the minister's opinion, I think, and that is mine.
When we were debating which of these three routes we should use the choice was left to the provinces, as it should have been.
Premier Manning and Mr. Carson, who then had responsibility in British Columbia, chose the central route. I believe that in making their choice as the ideal highway route they made a major blunder. I think the reason they selected the route-in fact I am almost certain of it-was that they wanted to see the dominion government get its teeth into that problem because in Alberta the highway had to go through the E.I.D., which is an irrigation problem and which is a very costly kind of terrain to take a highway through, while in British Columbia there are mountain difficulties on the Big Bend highway.
Anyway they selected that as the trans-Canada highway official route. We are still having troubles, and we are going to have plenty of troubles for a good many years yet before we find the really best central route to accept, as the hon. member for Kootenay West has just pointed out. Meanwhile the completion of the trans-Canada highway is awaiting all these decisions to be made.
The southernmost route is the Crowsnest route. That route is not so very difficult. There is much building already accomplished. In fact Alberta highway No. 3 now completed crosses the province of Alberta and gives a good highway right from the western border of Saskatchewan out to the border of British Columbia, and British Columbia has made splendid progress from the British Columbia eastern border west as far as Creston. I went over that section several times last year and I was struck with admiration for the very fine highway that is being built there.
Now British Columbia has built a great deal of good highway from Vancouver east. There is only one section of the Crowsnest route highway which it seems to me needs to be built at the present time to enable it to link right up and connect through to Vancouver, and that is the stretch between Creston and 

Trail. It is sometimes called the Creston-Salmo-Trail cut-off. I understand it will be expensive to build that highway, but that the route is thoroughly feasible and the highway can be built.
Last night the hon. member for Vancouver East mentioned the possibility of going down the eastern side of the Cascades into the United States, going along a corridor and coming up on the western side of those mountains. He mentioned that as being a desirable route. I have no objection to that suggestion, but with all due respect to the United States, I do not hesitate to say that we cannot safely bequeath to our children of the future any possibility of complications with that country. It will be good to make an arrangement with them so long as it is temporary; but if we are to be safe we must build in Canada, as well as the Creston-Salmo-Trail area so we might be sure we have a good highway in Canada. Then the United States will not bother us at all.
My suggestion to the minister would be that he give immediate attention to the construction in that area from Creston to Trail. If the British Columbia government needs assistance financially-and I am sure it does- I would suggest that he make an especial effort to provide financial assistance. Something like this might be done. Money might be taken out of the Bank of Canada at probably 1$ per cent interest and advanced to British Columbia with which British Columbia could finish that road right through, with the assistance, aid, advice and co-operation of the federal government.
This thing could be done on a basis like this. The province might have this money advanced without being considered to be indebted with interest attached, and it could pay off this money year by year as it felt able to spend the amount of money, so that in due time the money would be returned to the federal government, the province of British Columbia would own the highway outright and the highway at an early date would be complete.
I just want to say a word or two about the highway system. I do not want anyone to get the idea that I do not want to see the northern part of Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia served by the Yellowhead pass highway. It is an excellent highway, or will be when it is finished, and it is greatly needed. It also connects areas of great potential industrial and commercial importance. I do not want to see the central route neglected. I should like to see the Big Bend highway constructed just as soon as possible, but meanwhile I should like to say, in the words of the minister, that we must get this

highway or at least a highway through to Vancouver just as soon as we can possibly do it.
In order that this end may be accomplished,
I think the dominion government would be well advised to expand its program with respect to building highways for the especial benefit of the three western provinces so as to include a system of highways that will envisage the construction of three highways at least, and that the dominion government co-operate and assist in every way in the construction of all three. But let us concentrate on the southernmost one first, because 1 am sure it can be finished soon and is the best one, or will be ultimately.
There is one thing more about this southernmost route that I should mention. It is an all-weather highway. Very rarely do you find the road impassable right from Lethbridge or Medicine Hat clear on out to Vancouver. At such times as there may be obstruction as the result of snow, the situation can quite easily be taken care of by the snow-cleaning machinery which we have available at the present time. Concerning the other two highways I do not believe as good a report can be made.
Once more may I urge on the minister that without any further delay he go right to work on this matter of planning and building a system of highways across western Canada from Winnipeg to the city of Vancouver, especially concentrating upon the Crowsnest route.

I should like to ask the minister if there are any standards of construction with regard to the trans-Canada highway that are insisted upon by the federal government. I do so because of the experience in Manitoba, and I presume other provinces have had the same experience, that the construction of a road using bitumen or black top, as it is commonly called, involves very heavy maintenance costs, and it would seem
[Mr. Winters.!

that the only satisfactory material for the road is concrete? Are there any standards requiring a particular type of construction?

Yes, there are standards. The specifications permit either asphalt compound or concrete, and in the province of Manitoba good use is being made of concrete. Generally the standards are that there is to be a 24-foot paved surface, with a minimum of 22 feet, 10-foot shoulders on each side, 600-foot vertical and horizontal sight distances and other limitations of curvature. The specification does permit the minister responsible to authorize deviations from the specification where they are requested in writing and where economies or the topography of the situation seem to dictate deviations from the standards, but generally speaking we have been quite successful in having the provincial governments adhere to the standards to which they agreed.
Does the matter of the use of concrete rest with the provincial government?
Yes, it does.
