408. To provide for the expenses incurred by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in constructing and supervising construction of married quarters, rental housing, schools and related services on behalf of the Department of National Defence, $1,450,000.

This item has to do with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I have had a complaint from Vancouver to the effect that it is very difficult to get approval for a loan under the National Housing Act on a 33-foot lot. Perhaps I could best place the position before the minister by reading extracts from a letter I have received from a reliable person who is in touch with the situation. This gentleman says:
The point I want to bring to your notice is the difficulty of getting a 33-foot lot approved for an N.H.A. home. It is easy enough to get approval for a large lot for a home of anywhere from $13,000 to $20,000, and this is where the act misses the point:	A lot of these people don't need any help;
it's the young couple starting out in life who want to get a home that need the help.
Then he goes on to say:
I was dealing with a couple last week who are living in a basement suite. I found a lot, 33 feet, which is their limit financially; but because there were several vacant lots in the block it would be just a waste of time to try to get approval from the N.H.A. people. So we had to arrange for a private mortgage which means higher monthly payments and interest.
Then my correspondent goes on to say:
Yet on the other hand a man in the high income bracket can apply for an N.H.A. loan to build a duplex for revenue purposes, and get it every time.
Why is it so difficult in Vancouver to get approval for a loan where the home is being built on a 33-foot lot?

The same general regulations apply across the country. Part of the National Housing Act confers upon Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation the responsibility for encouraging a good class of housing in Canada, as well as developing the desired quantity of housing. In the light of experience to date it has been found that a house on a lot smaller than 40 feet is not the kind of house that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation would approve for mortgage purposes.
I do not think this works any great hardship. I have had no problem brought to my attention before. This is the first time I have heard this complaint, that we are not authorizing loans because the lot is too small.

My understanding is that the housing act was designed originally to help

Supply-Public Works
young people acquire homes. In Vancouver quite a large part of the city has been subdivided on a 33-foot lot basis. In recent years I believe a lot must be 40-feet, but in the old subdivisions the lots were all 33 feet. I think it is most unfortunate that a person with a family cannot get any help under the National Housing Act if he builds on a 33-foot lot. It is perfectly legal to have them, if the subdivision was made some years ago.
Lots in the city are now becoming very scarce. And, as my correspondent says, young people in this position many times cannot afford to buy bigger lots. Surely it is not the policy of the government that young people who do not have large sums of money cannot get any help. They are the ones who need it more than others. This is one situation the minister might check in order to see if there is not some way in which he can get around this difficulty.

As my hon. friend knows, the 33-foot lot certainly makes for congestion in the long run; and we have the responsibility of trying to develop projects that will stand for a long time as a credit to the communities. Most municipalities now have gone to a minimum 40-foot lot. Very few of them do not insist upon lot frontages larger than 33 feet in subdivisions, and I think it would be a mistake to encourage housing developments these days on a 33-foot lot basis. But if the hon. member will give me the particular case he has in mind I will look into it.
In Vancouver some of the finest people in the city started out in homes on 33-foot lots. The hon. member for Greenwood has just said to me that he is now living on a 33-foot lot.
Where?
In the slums of Toronto.

There are not many of these smaller sized lots left in Vancouver, but I see no reason why it should not be possible for the owner of a 33-foot lot to have the benefit of a loan under the National Housing Act.
Would the hon. member give me the details of the case he has in mind. Perhaps he would send it to me.

Apparently this is the general practice of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in Vancouver, namely that they will not approve a loan for a house on a 33-foot lot. It is that policy which I think should be made more flexible.
Exceptions are now made, but as a general policy we like to encourage a minimum 40-foot lot.
Exceptions are now being made, are they?
Yes.

I wish to bring a matter to the attention of the minister. I have been asked to do this by a member of an organization in Trail. I am referring to the proposed sale of the Sunningdale houses at Trail, British Columbia, which have been occupied by veteran tenants since 1948.
The sale of these houses has been the concern of these veteran tenants for a number of years. As the minister and his officials know, there has been considerable correspondence in this matter. The veterans were delighted to hear last year that there was a possibility the houses would be offered for sale this year. Finally there was a decision to sell on the part of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and at that time I received a letter from the minister in which he advised me that the houses were being offered for sale. He said in one paragraph:
Letters offering the houses for sale to the present tenants will be despatched on July 4th. The prices established by the corporation for the two-bedroom units, will be $5,950 to $6,250 and for the three-bedroom units, the prices will be $7,050 to $7,400. To the above prices is added a rebate of $1,000 which may be earned by the purchaser at the rate of $16.66 per month over a period of five years for each month of continued ownership and occupancy.
Shortly after that the tenants were advised, I think by Mr. Wood, branch manager of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in Trail. Then the storm blew up. First of all I received a strong protest from the city of Trail. I received the following letter from L. G. Anderson, city clerk:
Dear Sir:
We enclose herewith a copy of our letter to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation requesting that the sale price established on the low rental homes in Sunningdale be reviewed as it was the opinion of the tenants that these values are out of line.
Then I received a telegram from the Canadian Legion in Trail expressing strong dissatisfaction with the sale price:
Trail Branch No. 11, Canadian Legion strongly protests sale price set by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation re Sunningdale veterans homes. Any assistance you can give in this regard will be appreciated.
Then I received another telegram from the secretary of the committee which represents all these veteran tenants. These are very responsible people:
Sunningdale veterans protest ridiculously high prices set on houses. All our previous correspondence has been ignored. Urgent that you take action to correct this injustice.

And so on. Then the city clerk wrote a letter to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and I shall quote just a paragraph from that letter:
At the regular meeting of the council held July 4 a delegation, appointed by the tenants and represented by Mr. R. F. Harrison, addressed the council advising that in their opinion the sale price of the homes was too high. The delegation stated that a maximum sale price of $5,500 for the three-bedroom house and $5,100 for the two-bedroom house had been placed on the homes by a qualified statistician who based his findings on the type ol construction, age, and location of the dwellings.
It was also pointed out that the tenants had maintained and improved the properties at their own expense over the years, and that this factor should also be considered in setting a sale price.
It was further pointed out that by withholding the S1.000 rebate for a period of five years, the purchaser would be penalized due to the fact that interest would be charged on this sum for the five-year period and would result in the purchaser receiving a lesser rebate.
In view of the circumstances as outlined by the veteran tenants, it was the decision of the council that your corporation be asked to obtain the services of an impartial appraiser for the purpose of establishing a fair and equitable sale value of the homes.
The council has, on previous occasions, requested that the homes be made available for purchase by the tenants and, in further continuance of this desire, it would be appreciated if you would give this matter your earnest consideration.
My roint is this, Mr. Chairman. We have these three responsible organizations taking exception to the prices established; the city council of Trail, the Canadian Legion in Trail, a branch of over a thousand members, and then the committee of the Sunningdale veterans' housing project, which is a committee composed mostly of engineers employed by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, all responsible organizations and people who have some understanding of building and a good knowledge of sales.
In view of the fact that the minister on one occasion did tell us that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is not a profitmaking organization, will he consider the representations of these organizations and my representations this evening, and have an independent appraiser appointed to establish the real value of these houses? I trust that as a result a valuation will be established that will satisfy the tenants, the council, the Legion and all people concerned.

I understand the hon. member for Kootenay West would like me to reply.
This question has come up in the house before. There are a number of municipalities, some 23 in all, where the veterans' houses have been put up for sale at th : request of the veterans themselves. The government has not been anxious to sell these houses. We have put them in what we term a sales position in order to meet the express wishes
Supply-Public Works
of the veterans themselves and local organizations. We have in no instances endeavoured to push these sales. It is a matter left entirely to the individual veterans themselves to decide whether they wish to buy. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is endeavouring to do no more than have its costs returned. It is not making any profit at all on the transaction.
The hon. member has referred to the fact that these people have kept their houses in good condition and in some instances have improved them. 1 agree that they have done so, and it is to their credit; but it must be remembered that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, during the period in question, has had considerable administrative costs, and during this period the veteran tenants have been getting good accommodation at a low rental. I think that in itself leads them to believe that they should be permitted to buy these houses at a lower price than they are offered.
I understand that in Trail a house of the type that is being offered for sale would cost at least $3,000 more than they are being offered by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. To date, despite the fact that no sales effort has been put into this program -in fact, as I said before, the government is not pushing it but simply endeavouring to meet the wishes of those veterans who have indicated a desire to buy the houses-279 of them have been sold, and in the month of June just past 66 houses moved into the hands of veteran owners. I think that is an indication that the over-all program is acceptable and that it is generally fair.
That is all across Canada?
All across Canada, yes.

May I ask the minister a question with regard to his statement that Sir Robert Borden's statue, as I understand it, is to be placed west of the west block? Does the minister think that is like putting it in no-man's land? That part of the grounds is never frequented and it will never be seen. I submit that for consideration.
The item has been disposed of, and we are on housing now, Mr. Chairman. I thought it met with the approval of the Leader of the Opposition. Certainly he was a party to discussions about the statue.
No, I was not a party to any discussion of location.

I thought it was mentioned at the time we were together. If the Leader of the Opposition says no, I accept that. However, I believe the location to the west of the west block near the driveway leading out

Supply-Public Works to the west gate is a prominent location. It is intended that it balance up the statues on the east side of the east block. I personally feel it is quite an appropriate location, and I thought it was generally accepted.

When the Minister of National Health and Welfare had his estimates before us the other night there was some discussion about housing for the aged. At this point the Minister of Public Works might have something to say.
I am very glad the minister is now providing some subsidized low rental housing. We have a very large group of Canadians in the old age pension bracket. In all the provinces where there are Liberal governments we find there are no supplementary benefits paid, which would indicate that in those provinces at least it is considered that those who are receiving old age pensions are federal responsibilities.
Would the minister indicate what stage he has reached in studying the problem to find out how large a group we have in Canada who are receiving old age pensions, and what sort of housing a couple getting $80 a month are able to obtain? Can he give us some information as to the sort of housing that is available in cities like Toronto, Montreal and Halifax for a couple receiving $40 a month each? Has the time not arrived when the minister should be entering the field of low rental subsidized housing in co-operation with the provinces and municipalities for those people receiving old age pensions, the group 70 or over?
I am referring to a couple who receive $80 a month and who have no other income. They should be able to get some housing. Will the minister say what studies are being carried on and how soon he would be prepared to recommend that subsidies be paid by the federal government to make housing possible for people in this group?

I do not know what significance the hon. member intended by his statement that no Liberal government pays supplementary benefits. I am sure he has full knowledge of the fact that it was a Liberal government which made old age pensions available right across Canada.
But some provinces are paying supplementary grants, like Saskatchewan and Alberta.
The basic arrangement was put into effect by a Liberal government.
Nothing more than $40.

Be that as it may, the subject under consideration is housing, particularly for the aged and those who are not able to


pay economic rentals. I am sure my hon. friend is familiar with the old section 36 of the National Housing Act, which enables us to enter into partnership arrangements with any provincial government that cares to do so to provide subsidized housing for the citizens of municipalities within the province. That program has worked out quite well. It has been implemented to the greatest extent in Ontario, but other provinces including Saskatchewan have taken advantage of it.
There is also the limited dividend section of the act which has been used in Saskatchewan, British Columbia and elsewhere with particular application to old age pensioners. It enables interested bodies to make available low rental housing to old age pensioners without the subsidy element. If a provincial government is interested in going beyond that and getting into the subsidization realm of housing, then section 36 is available. We have invited them on more than one occasion.
Would the minister indicate how many units have been constructed in Canada which are available to the old age pension group?
I am informed that a rough estimate would be somewhere around 2,000 under the limited dividend section covering low rental housing.
